paragraphs: The wall was done, the people had promised to follow God, and then Nehemiah went away for a while. Look what he found when he came back: the storerooms of God's house had been turned into a guest room, the Levites had gone back to their fields, and the Sabbath had turned into market day (Nehemiah 13:5, 10, 15). I can't judge anybody, friend. I once let a whole drawer of dust pile up on me and called it "settling in." Drift doesn't announce itself. It just moves in quietly, one little yes at a time.

So here's what I want you to catch. Nehemiah didn't just get upset. He acted. He threw out what didn't belong, put the Levites back at their posts, shut the gates, and asked the nobles, "What is this evil you are doing…" (Nehemiah 13:17). I think what this passage is showing us is that a promise made to God has to be lived out again and again, and some days that means doing the hard, unpopular thing. Some of what happened here was heavy, and the Bible doesn't hide that.

And listen to how Nehemiah keeps praying. Over and over he prays, "Remember me," and he ends with, "Remember me, O my God, with favor" (Nehemiah 13:14, 22, 31). Notice he asks God not to blot out his deeds of loving devotion, and he also asks for mercy "according to Your abundant loving devotion" (Nehemiah 13:14, 22). That's the lesson, baker: keep your heart close to God's Word, keep fixing what has drifted, and trust His mercy to hold you up. The story of Nehemiah ends here, but the ovens stay warm and the Word keeps teaching.
